subsystems.name: Spin cell
subsystems.role: sealed chamber holding the noble-gas isotopes that do the sensing, plus a trace of alkali metal vapour to connect them to the laser light.
parts: micromachined silicon or glass body with bonded windows
noble-gas isotopes such as xenon-129, xenon-131 or helium-3
anti-relaxation wall coating or buffer gas

subsystems.name: Optical pumping
subsystems.role: circularly polarised laser light aligns the alkali-metal electron spins, and collisions then transfer that alignment to the noble-gas nuclei.

subsystems.name: Magnetic bias and coil set
subsystems.role: provides the steady, highly uniform field that sets the nuclear precession frequency, plus pulses that tip the spins.
parts: precision coil sets for bias, trim gradients and radio-frequency drive

subsystems.name: Magnetic shielding and thermal control
subsystems.role: stops the outside magnetic field and temperature changes from corrupting the measurement.

subsystems.name: Readout
subsystems.role: senses the precession of the noble-gas spins as a phase that race against the drive field.
parts: probe laser with a balanced polarimeter (Faraday rotation)

subsystems.name: Signal processing and control
subsystems.role: turns the two precession signals into an angular rate.
parts: dual-isotope differencing that cancels magnetic drift

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the spin cell
buildSteps.detail: A silicon or glass body a few millimetres to a few centimetres across is patterned, filled with the isotope mixture and a small alkali-metal ampoule, then sealed by anodic bonding or glassblowing so the gas stays pure for years.

buildSteps.title: Treat the cell walls
buildSteps.detail: The inner surface is coated or a buffer gas added so that a nucleus survives thousands of wall collisions before losing its spin, because that lifetime sets the sensor's sensitivity.

buildSteps.title: Build the magnetic assembly
buildSteps.detail: Nested mu-metal shields are formed and annealed, then coil forms are wound and aligned so the bias field is uniform to a part in a million across the cell.

buildSteps.title: Integrate the optics
buildSteps.detail: Laser, polariser, wave plate and photodetector are mounted around the cell and aligned so the pump beam and probe beam cross within the gas volume; the whole head sits in a temperature-stabilised oven.

buildSteps.title: Polarise and tune
buildSteps.detail: The laser is tuned to the alkali absorption line and the gas is spin-polarised; the bias field is then adjusted so the two isotopes precess at known, widely separated frequencies.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate against rotation
buildSteps.detail: The sealed sensor is mounted on a rate table. Rotation is applied and the isotope difference is measured, giving the scale factor and letting the electronics lock onto the precession.

buildSteps.title: Characterise drift
buildSteps.detail: The unit is run for hours to days on a stable platform to measure bias stability, angle random walk, scale-factor linearity and sensitivity to temperature and magnetic fields.

buildSteps.title: Qualify and package into an inertial unit
buildSteps.detail: The sensor head is shock-, vibration- and thermal-cycled, then combined with accelerometers and a stable clock to form a navigation-grade inertial measurement unit.

prerequisites.why: wafer-level cells with alkali metal inside are already made for miniature atomic clocks and magnetometers; the hard part is keeping nuclear spin alive in a tiny volume.
the technique for transferring laser polarisation to noble-gas nuclei is routine in polarised-gas production, though it normally uses much larger cells and lasers.
the pump light must sit precisely on the alkali absorption line and stay there as temperature drifts.

prerequisites.tech: Precision magnetic shielding and coil drives
prerequisites.why: residual field drift is the dominant error; shielding and low-noise currents hold it below the level that would otherwise swamp the rotation signal.
using two isotopes with different gyromagnetic ratios to separate rotation from magnetic drift is demonstrated but is only now being engineered into a rugged, manufacturable sensor.

pathway.milestone: laboratory and defence-funded prototypes reporting navigation-grade bias stability in a compact head
pathway.unlocks: confidence that the spin physics survives miniaturisation and that the error budget closes.

pathway.milestone: ruggedised, qualified sensor heads that hold calibration through military shock, vibration and temperature cycling
pathway.unlocks: first operational trials in vehicles that cannot rely on satellite navigation.

pathway.milestone: multisensor inertial navigation: these gyroscopes combined with accelerometers and a compact atomic clock, drifting only slowly over days
pathway.unlocks: long-endurance underwater and high-latitude navigation without satellite fixes.

pathway.milestone: volume manufacturing that brings cost down to compete with ring-laser and fibre-optic gyroscopes
pathway.unlocks: wider use in aircraft, spacecraft and survey work, wherever a long, uninterrupted attitude and heading reference is needed.
